To put it another way, perhaps it is appropriate to
say that the early church fathers viewed pseudepigrapha as we view
works today which claim to be written by someone they are not: lying.
Pseudepigrapha is lying. There is more to say about this, but what
I
want to impress upon the reader is this:
The claim that pseudepigrapha was willingly accepted into the
New Testament by early church fathers is wrong.
In my opinion, there is no way around this. Either 1 and 2 Peter
were written by Peter and should be canonical, or it is pseudepigrapha
and the early church fathers were deceived.
Without Petrine
authorship, I must agree with G. Klein who “say[s] that it is unfortunate
the letter was even included in the canon.”
If 1 and 2 Peter were not
written by the apostle Peter, then the early church fathers
got it wrong
And if that is the case, 1 and 2 Peter ought not be found within the
bounds of our NT.
Do you, the reader, now see the seriousness of canonicity in
regard to the discussion of 1 and 2 Peter? The discussion of the
authorship of these two letters is bigger than simply “Bible trivia.” This
is a matter of what books we believe are canonical and,
by extension,
inspired and therefore God’s word.
Bilingualism
Bilingualism
Let us begin examining more specific evidence for Petrine authorship.
Before we can even evaluate the evidence from the text itself, we must
begin with the most fundamental question:
Could Peter even speak
Greek?
(Mark 5:41)
Literacy in Galilee: Could Peter Read and Write?

the testament genre and known Peter did not write it. My question: Where is the evidence of this
claim? If Bauckham is correct, why is there so much debate over authe
nticity rather than a more
outspoken voice saying, “This is written in the testament genre and not by the apostle Peter”? See
Schreiner’s discussion of the testament genre in which he deems Bauckham’s theory as failed, T.

1, 2 Peter, and Jude
276. Guthrie concludes his discussion of pseudepigraphy by
saying, “The only conclusion to which the evidence would seem to point is that if pseudepigrapha
must on the basis of criticism be admitted within the New Testament canon, they must have been
received without their recipients being aware of their true character. If this is a valid conclusion the
charge of deliberate deception can scarcely be avoided.” See R. Guthrie,
